rows.description: A child sees a friend take the last turn on the swing and feels a hot jolt of unfairness. He says "That's mine" louder than needed, already sure the other child did it on purpose.
graph_context: next stage: Blame and counter-blame
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: Each child recounts the story so that only the other is at fault. Voices rise, "you always" and "you never" appear, and neither is listening because both are busy preparing the next defence.
graph_context: previous stage: Small trigger
next stage: Raising the stakes
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: Feeling cornered before an audience, the child drags in old grievances and insults the friend's family or looks. Winning starts to matter more than the swing, and the words chosen are meant to hurt.
graph_context: previous stage: Blame and counter-blame
next stage: Flooding
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: grief, hurt

rows.description: The child on the receiving end has a racing heart and hot face, and can no longer think straight. He either shoves, cries, or storms off, which is the body taking over rather than a considered choice.
graph_context: previous stage: Raising the stakes
next stage: Adult or peer pause
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: overwhelm

rows.description: A teacher separates them without ruling on who won, and lets each cool down with water or a walk. Calm comes first; only then does she ask each child for their version and what they were feeling.
graph_context: previous stage: Flooding
next stage: Naming the need and settling
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: calm

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Naming the need and settling [Response]
rows.description: Children who have cooled can say "I felt cheated" instead of "you cheat" and agree a turn-taking rule. The turning point is swapping who is right for what is fair, and both usually feel lighter afterwards.
graph_context: previous stage: Adult or peer pause
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Public teasing meets a raw spot [Receiver]
rows.description: In the group chat a teenager is teased about his marks, and it lands on a fear that he is not good enough. He replies quickly, before thinking, because silence would feel like admitting it.
graph_context: next stage: Audience effect
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: fear

rows.description: Classmates start reacting with emojis and screenshots, and the argument becomes a show. Both teens now defend their reputation with an audience watching, which makes backing down feel like a public loss.
graph_context: previous stage: Public teasing meets a raw spot
next stage: Escalation by allies
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22

rows.description: Friends join in on each side and repeat things said in private. What was a two-person quarrel becomes two camps, and the original hurt is buried under loyalty and taking sides.
graph_context: previous stage: Audience effect
next stage: Exhaustion and second thoughts
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: hurt

rows.description: After a day of sulking the teen realises he is more hurt about being laughed at than about anything said. The anger drains, and he wonders how to step back without looking weak.
graph_context: previous stage: Escalation by allies
next stage: One person moves first
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: amusement, anger, curiosity, tiredness
